E048-01.notes: Subordinating 'when' introduces a clause and takes no comma after it. A puts a comma after 'when'; C's semicolon leaves a fragment; D splits subject from verb. Facts check out: Silver overheard the request at Drexel in 1948, Woodland learned Morse code as a Boy Scout, and the idea came on Miami Beach.

E048-02.notes: 'just as' sets up the parallel comparison cleanly. B 'just like how' is wordy and informal; C 'the same as when' wrongly adds time; D 'as if' makes it hypothetical and changes the meaning.

E048-03.notes: Getting a patent and still having equipment too expensive for stores is a contrast. B, C and D all say cause and effect, which is illogical: the patent did not make the equipment expensive. Fact: patent US 2,612,994 was issued Oct. 7, 1952 for the bull's-eye design, so this is accurate.

flags.note: The current placement splits the cause-effect chain (6 'equipment ... too expensive' -> 8 'the idea sat unused ... no practical way to scan'), so A is not a clearly seamless spot. C (before 6) is somewhat defensible: it would describe the design right before 'received a patent for their design.' It loses because 'Their' would follow a paragraph that refers only to 'he' (Woodland), so the pronoun lacks a clear antecedent at a paragraph start. Consider tightening sentence 7, e.g. 'Their patented version ...', or recasting 8 so it links back to cost.

E048-04.notes: 'Their version' needs 'Woodland and Silver ... their design' in sentence 6 as its antecedent, so it belongs right after 6. B (after 8) leaves the design detail stranded after the dormancy. D (after 10) is wrong because the UPC scanned in 1974 used straight bars, not circles. Fact check: bull's-eye readable from any direction is accurate.
